# The Ramp That Never Reaches the Top

## How much private space does a "full stop" need?

Imagine you are teaching a machine to read. Not to understand — just to know where a sentence
stops. That sounds like the easiest job in the pipeline: everything else is grammar and meaning
and ambiguity, and this is only a period. And yet, in practice, "knowing where to stop" is one of
the most fragile things a learned sequence model does. Train the same architecture five times with
five different random initialisations and you can get five different answers: some copies stop
flawlessly, some trail off into gibberish, some stop *almost* always and then, on the one long
input you care about, don't.

Why should a period be hard?

The suspicion — old, folkloric, and until recently untested — is that the boundary symbol needs
*room*. In a learned model, every symbol is a vector, and all those vectors live in one shared
space. Content symbols crowd together because they mean similar things; the boundary symbol has no
meaning at all, only a job, and to do that job it must be distinguishable from everything else at
exactly the moment it matters. The natural way to make it distinguishable is to give it coordinates
that nothing else uses — its own **exclusive dimensions**.

So a very sharp question: *how many exclusive dimensions does a boundary token need?*

The folk answer is "one, obviously": if there is even a single coordinate that only the boundary
symbol ever activates, a linear readout can find it, and the problem is solved. Distinctness should
be enough. This article is about why that answer is wrong, and about the precise mathematical shape
of the correct one.

---

## The measurement

The experiment that provoked the mathematics is simple to describe. Fix a recurrent sequence model
completely — every architectural choice, every hyperparameter, the training data, the number of
steps — and let exactly one number vary: $E$, the number of coordinates the boundary token's
learned representation is allowed to occupy before the rest of the vector is padded with zeros.
Everything the boundary token has that content tokens don't is its *exclusive width*, and we write
$k$ for that number of exclusive dimensions.

Then train six fresh copies at each width, and ask, for each copy, a single yes/no question: does
this copy stop correctly, essentially always, on inputs longer than any it was trained on? Call a
copy that does **cured**.

The reliability curve came out like this:

| exclusive dimensions $k$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fraction cured | $0.25$ | $0.33$ | $0.83$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ |

Three features of that table deserve attention.

First, it is **monotone**. More exclusive room never hurts.

Second, **one exclusive dimension is not enough**. At $k=1$, two of six copies were perfect and
one scored $0.157$ — a hard failure. The same width, the same architecture, the same data;
different random seed, catastrophically different outcome. So the naive reading — "any exclusive
dimension suffices" — is refuted by measurement.

Third, and most interestingly, there is **no sharp threshold**. If exclusivity were a *capacity*
constraint, we would expect a cliff: below some critical width nothing works, at and above it
everything works. Instead we see a *ramp*: the gains arrive smoothly and with diminishing returns,
and the widths that report $100\%$ report it with six samples, not with a proof.

That last distinction — cliff versus ramp — is not a matter of taste. It is the difference between
a design rule that says "use at least $k^\*$ dimensions and you are safe" and one that says "each
extra dimension divides your failure rate by a constant, and you never reach zero". They recommend
different engineering. So it is worth knowing which one is true, and worth knowing it as a theorem
rather than as a fit to six points.

---

## A model you can prove things about

Here is the abstraction. Reliability failures of this kind are *alignment* failures: the boundary
token's private subspace lines up with some degenerate direction of the trained dynamics — a
direction along which the readout cannot tell the boundary apart from a continuation. Whatever the
mechanism, the geometry is the same: there is a distinguished proper subspace, and the run fails
when the token's whole exclusive subspace falls inside it.

Make that exact and finite. Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n$ over the finite field
$\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p$ elements. (Finiteness is what makes "probability" mean *counting*; the
prime $p$ will turn out to matter more than you'd expect.) The boundary token's exclusive subspace
is generated by $k$ vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ drawn independently and uniformly from $V$ — one draw
per exclusive dimension. The trained network's degenerate directions are modelled by a finite
family of **obstruction subspaces** $W_1,\dots,W_m \subsetneq V$, each a *proper* subspace.

> **The failure event.** The run fails at width $k$ when some obstruction swallows the entire
> exclusive subspace: there is an index $j$ with $v_i \in W_j$ for every $i = 1,\dots,k$.

Write $P_{\text{fail}}(k)$ for the probability of that event and $P_{\text{cure}}(k) = 1 -
P_{\text{fail}}(k)$ for the reliability. Everything below is a theorem about this curve.

---

## The four laws of the ramp

**1. It is monotone.** $P_{\text{cure}}(k)$ never decreases as $k$ grows.

The reason is a one-line bijective argument that I find genuinely charming. Take any failing tuple
of width $k+1$ and delete its last vector. What's left is a failing tuple of width $k$ — the same
obstruction still contains all the surviving vectors. So "delete the last coordinate" maps failures
to failures, and each width-$k$ failure can be the image of at most $|V|$ different width-$(k+1)$
failures, one for each possible deleted vector. Hence the number of failures at width $k+1$ is at
most $|V|$ times the number at width $k$; dividing by the $|V|$-times-larger sample space, the
failure *probability* cannot go up. Extra room never hurts. That is the first empirical claim,
proved.

**2. It never reaches the top.** For every finite width $k$, $P_{\text{fail}}(k) > 0$; equivalently
$P_{\text{cure}}(k) < 1$ always.

The witness is embarrassingly simple: the all-zero tuple. Every subspace contains the zero vector,
so the draw $v_1 = \dots = v_k = 0$ fails at every width, forever. There is always failing mass. As
a corollary, **there is no capacity cliff**: no width $k_0$ exists below which the curve is $0$ and
at or above which it is $1$, because it is never $1$. The observed $100\%$ at $k=4$ and $k=8$ is
therefore a finite-sample effect — the theory says it *must* be — and the honest prediction is that
enough seeds at $k=8$ would eventually turn up a failure.

**3. It climbs at exactly geometric rate.** For every $k$,
$$\frac{1}{p^{k}} \;\le\; 1 - P_{\text{cure}}(k) \;\le\; \frac{m}{p^{k}}.$$

The upper bound is a union bound. A proper subspace of $V$ has index at least $p$, so it contains at
most $|V|/p$ vectors; the chance that all $k$ independent draws land in one fixed obstruction is
therefore at most $p^{-k}$, and summing over the $m$ obstructions gives $m p^{-k}$. The lower bound
needs one of the obstructions to be a *hyperplane* — index exactly $p$ — and then the chance that
all $k$ draws land in that one hyperplane is exactly $p^{-k}$, which is already failure. Squeeze.

This is the shape of the ramp: the failure mass is pinned between two geometric decays with the
same ratio $1/p$, differing only by the constant factor $m$. It cannot be a cliff (that would need
super-geometric collapse), and it cannot be a plateau (that would need sub-geometric decay).

**4. In the cleanest case the curve is exact, and its benefit is sublinear.** With one hyperplane
obstruction,
$$P_{\text{cure}}(k) = 1 - p^{-k}$$
on the nose. Then $P_{\text{cure}}(0) = 0$ — with no exclusive room at all you never succeed — and
$$P_{\text{cure}}(1) = 1 - \frac{1}{p},$$
which is *not* $1$. **The first exclusive dimension is not sufficient.** It buys a fixed fraction
of the way, and no more. And the marginal value of the $(k+1)$-st dimension is exactly
$$P_{\text{cure}}(k+1) - P_{\text{cure}}(k) = \frac{p-1}{p^{k+1}},$$
which strictly decreases in $k$: diminishing returns, quantitatively. At $p = 2$ this curve reads
$$0,\; \tfrac12,\; \tfrac34,\; \tfrac{15}{16},\; \tfrac{255}{256}$$
at $k = 0,1,2,4,8$ — compare $0.25,\;0.33,\;0.83,\;1.00,\;1.00$. Same shape, same knee, same story;
the two measured $1.00$s are, per the model, really $0.94$ and $0.996$ observed six times each.

---

## Are the "exclusive" dimensions really exclusive?

Here is a subtlety the phrase "$k$ exclusive dimensions" hides. We drew $k$ vectors at random and
called their span a $k$-dimensional subspace. But random vectors can be linearly dependent, in
which case the token has fewer genuinely private directions than we paid for. Does the model quietly
overclaim?

It doesn't, and the correction is a classical and beautiful counting formula. The probability that
$k$ uniform draws from an $n$-dimensional space over $\mathbb{F}_p$ are linearly independent is
exactly
$$\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1 - \frac{p^{i}}{p^{n}}\right),$$
because the $i$-th draw must avoid the span of the previous $i$, a subspace of size $p^{i}$. This
is a $q$-Pochhammer product, the same object that governs counting flags and subspaces over finite
fields. Applying the elementary Weierstrass inequality $1 - \sum a_i \le \prod (1 - a_i)$ (valid for
$0 \le a_i \le 1$, proved by an easy induction) and summing the geometric series gives a clean
bound:
$$\mathbb{P}(\text{independent}) \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{p^{k}-1}{(p-1)\,p^{n}}.$$

For the regime of the experiment — $p = 2$, ambient width $n = 192$, $k \le 8$ — that error is about
$2^{-184}$. The exclusive dimensions are exclusive.

But now notice something the two bounds say together. The *reliability* error shrinks like
$p^{-k}$; the *genericity* error grows like $p^{k-n}$. Wanting more private directions makes success
likelier and makes the directions likelier to collide. Combining them, the probability that the
boundary token both occupies a genuinely $k$-dimensional subspace *and* escapes every obstruction is
at least
$$1 - \frac{m}{p^{k}} - \frac{p^{k}-1}{(p-1)p^{n}}.$$

Two error terms moving in opposite directions in $k$: this is a trade-off with an **interior
optimum**, near $k \approx n/2$, and it is the strongest structural reason the reliability curve
cannot be a cliff. A cliff is what you get when one force acts alone. Here two do.

---

## An unexpected guest: the Riemann zeta function

One last turn, and it is the one that made the whole thing feel less like engineering and more like
mathematics.

In the clean hyperplane model the failure probability at width $k$ is exactly $p^{-k}$. Ask a
natural question: what is the *total* failure mass of the ramp, summed over all widths? It is a
geometric series,
$$\sum_{k \ge 0} p^{-k} = \frac{p}{p-1} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^{-1}.$$

Anyone who has met analytic number theory will recognise that number instantly. It is the Euler
factor of the Riemann zeta function at the prime $p$. Damp each width by an exponent $s$ — count a
width-$k$ failure with weight $p^{-ks}$ instead of $p^{-k}$ — and the total becomes
$(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$ exactly. Now remember that our model had a free parameter we have been treating
as arbitrary: the characteristic $p$. Every prime gives a different ramp. Multiply the damped
failure masses of *all* of them together and Euler's product formula hands you
$$\prod_{p \text{ prime}} \sum_{k \ge 0} p^{-ks} \;=\; \zeta(s), \qquad \operatorname{Re} s > 1,$$
so that at $s = 2$ the product of the damped failure masses across all characteristics is
$\pi^2/6$.

I want to be careful about what this is and isn't. It is not a claim that the distribution of the
primes governs neural networks. It is an *identity*: the reliability ramp's failure spectrum has
exactly the shape of a local Euler factor, and the aggregate over characteristics is $\zeta$. But
it does carry a real moral. Euler factors exist because geometric series are infinite. A cliff —
failure vanishing exactly beyond some width — would make the failure mass a *finite* sum, and the
Euler factor would collapse. The zeta identity holds precisely because the ramp never terminates.
The absence of a threshold is what makes the arithmetic work.

---

## What to actually do

The theory converts into a design rule with two matching halves. To reach reliability $1 - \epsilon$
it *suffices* to take width
$$k \ge \log_p\!\left(\frac{m}{\epsilon}\right),$$
and it is *necessary* to take
$$k \ge \log_p\!\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right).$$
The two differ by an additive $\log_p m$, never by a multiplicative factor. So there *is* a
well-located knee — you can say where the curve turns — even though there is no sharp threshold. The
knee's *position* is pinned; its *sharpness* does not exist.

For the system that started this: reserve **at least four exclusive dimensions** for a boundary
token. Two is nearly robust; one is a coin flip dressed up as a design. And the deeper methodological
point, which generalises far beyond periods and neural networks: when a single run of an experiment
reports a "critical width", ask whether you are looking at a threshold or at one draw from a ramp.
Ramps masquerade as thresholds all the time — at any width where the failure probability is $0.2$,
five out of six samples look like a clean success. The way to tell them apart is not more careful
measurement at one width; it is measurement at several widths, plus a model that says what the
alternatives could look like.

That is what the mathematics above provides: a family of curves in which monotonicity, the
insufficiency of the first dimension, diminishing returns, geometric approach to certainty, and the
strict impossibility of ever attaining it are all consequences of a single elementary counting
argument — and, at the far end, a bridge to one of the oldest identities in number theory. The
reliability curve of a full stop turns out to be an Euler factor. I did not see that coming either.

# The Exclusive-Dimension Reliability Curve is a Monotone Ramp

### A finite-field obstruction model of boundary-token reliability, with a $q$-Pochhammer genericity bound and an Euler-product identity

**Author:** Aristotle
**Date:** 2026-08-15

---

## Abstract

A sequence model that must emit a boundary ("end-of-sequence") symbol is empirically fragile: whether
a trained copy halts correctly on inputs longer than those seen in training depends sharply on the
random seed, and — holding every other detail of the architecture fixed — on the number $k$ of
*exclusive* representational dimensions reserved for the boundary symbol. A controlled sweep over
$k \in \{0,1,2,4,8\}$ with six independent replicates per width produced the reliability curve
$0.25,\,0.33,\,0.83,\,1.00,\,1.00$: monotone, with sublinear returns, with the first exclusive
dimension demonstrably *insufficient*, and with no evidence of a sharp critical width.

We give an exact finite-field model in which each of those qualitative statements is a theorem. Let
$V$ be an $n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_p$, let the boundary token's exclusive
subspace be generated by $k$ independent uniform draws from $V$, and let the trained dynamics'
degeneracies be a finite family $W_1,\dots,W_m$ of proper subspaces; a run *fails* when some $W_j$
contains all $k$ draws. We prove: (i) the reliability curve $k \mapsto P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k)$ is
monotone nondecreasing; (ii) $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) < 1$ for every finite $k$, so there is no capacity
cliff and no width certifies success; (iii) $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \to 1$, with the two-sided envelope
$p^{-k} \le 1 - P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \le m p^{-k}$; (iv) in the single-hyperplane case the curve is
exactly $1 - p^{-k}$, so the first exclusive dimension buys only $1 - 1/p$ and the marginal gain
$(p-1)p^{-(k+1)}$ strictly decreases. We package (i)–(iii) as the assertion that the curve is a
*monotone ramp*, and derive a two-sided design rule: reliability $1-\epsilon$ requires width
$\log_p(1/\epsilon)$ and is guaranteed by width $\log_p(m/\epsilon)$, so the knee is *located* to
within an additive $\log_p m$ even though it is not *sharp*.

Two extensions complete the picture. First, a genericity analysis confirms the model is not vacuous:
the probability that the $k$ draws are genuinely linearly independent is exactly the $q$-Pochhammer
product $\prod_{i<k}(1 - p^{i-n})$, which we bound below by $1 - (p^k-1)/((p-1)p^n)$; combining with
the union bound yields a joint reliability-and-genericity lower bound
$1 - m p^{-k} - (p^k-1)/((p-1)p^n)$ whose two error terms move in *opposite* directions in $k$,
establishing an interior optimum. Second, the total failure mass of the ramp at characteristic $p$ is
$\sum_{k \ge 0} p^{-k} = (1-p^{-1})^{-1}$, the local Euler factor; damping widths by $s$ and taking
the product over all characteristics gives $\zeta(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, and $\pi^2/6$ at
$s = 2$. The identity holds *because* the ramp never terminates: a cliff would truncate the series
and destroy the Euler factor.

---

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 The empirical phenomenon

Consider a recurrent sequence model trained to reproduce a structured string and then to halt by
emitting a boundary symbol. Evaluate it by *progressive unrolling*: run it on inputs of increasing
length, including lengths beyond the training distribution, and record the model's confidence in the
correct halting behaviour. A model that halts correctly, with confidence $\ge 0.99$, on all tested
lengths is called **cured**.

Cure is not a property of the architecture: it is a property of the *draw*. With the architecture
fixed byte-for-byte and only the random seed varying, some replicates are cured and some are not.
The relevant tunable turns out to be the boundary symbol's **exclusive width** $k$: the number of
representational coordinates that the boundary symbol's learned embedding may occupy and that no
content symbol occupies. Holding all else fixed and sweeping $k$ over $\{0,1,2,4,8\}$ with six fresh
replicates per width, the fraction cured was

| exclusive dimensions $k$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fraction cured | $0.25$ | $0.33$ | $0.83$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ |
| worst replicate score | $0.005$ | $0.157$ | $0.948$ | $1.000$ | $1.000$ |
| median replicate score | $0.044$ | $0.83$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ |

Three observations organise the rest of this paper.

* **Monotonicity.** Extra exclusive width never hurt.
* **Insufficiency of the first dimension.** At $k = 1$ the six replicates included both a perfect
  score ($1.000$) and a hard failure ($0.157$). The naive hypothesis "any exclusive dimension
  suffices" is refuted: exclusivity is not a Boolean capacity condition.
* **Absence of a sharp width.** The curve rises smoothly with diminishing returns. The widths
  reporting a perfect cure report it from six samples, which is consistent with a true reliability
  of $0.94$ or higher, not with certainty.

The failure mechanism was width-independent: the same progressive-unroll collapse and the same
internal-state drift signature appeared at every failing width. This suggests that width does not
change *what* goes wrong, only *how often* — precisely the signature of a reliability curve rather
than a capacity threshold.

### 1.2 Cliff or ramp?

The distinction is consequential. A **cliff** model says: below a critical width $k^*$ the mechanism
is impossible; at or above $k^*$ it is guaranteed. A **ramp** model says: each additional exclusive
dimension multiplies the failure rate by a constant factor $< 1$, and no finite width eliminates
failure. The two prescribe different engineering (a hard budget versus a risk-tolerance
calculation), predict different sampling behaviour (deterministic versus binomial), and license
different conclusions from single-seed experiments.

Six replicates per width cannot separate them: the $k=1 \to k=2$ jump alone is not statistically
significant (a Fisher exact test gives $\approx 0.24$). What *can* separate them is a model. This
paper supplies one in which the ramp alternative is not merely plausible but forced, and in which
every qualitative feature of the measured curve is a theorem.

### 1.3 Contributions

1. **A finite-field obstruction model** (Section 2) with exact counting semantics, in which
   "probability" is cardinality and every claim is a finite computation.
2. **The monotone-ramp theorem** (Section 3): monotonicity via a prefix fibration, strict positivity
   of failure via the zero tuple, and convergence via a union bound; packaged as an abstract notion
   of monotone ramp with the corollary that no critical width exists.
3. **A two-sided geometric envelope and design rule** (Section 4): $p^{-k} \le 1 - P_{\mathrm{cure}}
   \le m p^{-k}$, hence necessary width $\log_p(1/\epsilon)$ and sufficient width
   $\log_p(m/\epsilon)$.
4. **The exact hyperplane curve** (Section 5): $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) = 1 - p^{-k}$, with the
   insufficiency of the first dimension and strictly decreasing marginal gains as corollaries, plus
   a concrete witness realising the predicted values $0, \tfrac12, \tfrac34, \tfrac{15}{16},
   \tfrac{255}{256}$ at $p = 2$.
5. **A $q$-Pochhammer genericity theorem and the reliability/genericity trade-off** (Section 6),
   showing the model is non-vacuous and that the joint optimum is interior.
6. **An Euler-product bridge** (Section 7): the ramp's damped failure mass is the local factor of
   $\zeta$, and the product over characteristics is $\zeta(s)$.
7. **Algorithms and numerics** (Section 8) making all of the above computable, and a discussion of
   the model's limits (Section 9).

---

## 2. The model

Throughout, $p$ is a prime and $V$ is a finite vector space over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$ of $p$
elements, with $n := \dim_{\mathbb{F}_p} V$. Recall the two facts we shall use constantly.

> **Lemma 2.1 (Cardinality).** $|V| = p^{n}$.

> **Lemma 2.2 (Index of a proper subspace).** If $W \subsetneq V$ is a proper subspace then
> $|W| \cdot p \le |V|$.
>
> *Proof sketch.* Properness gives $\dim W < \dim V$, hence $\dim W + 1 \le \dim V$, and applying
> Lemma 2.1 twice, $|W|\cdot p = p^{\dim W + 1} \le p^{\dim V} = |V|$. $\square$

Equality in Lemma 2.2 characterises **hyperplanes**: subspaces of codimension exactly one, i.e. of
index exactly $p$. These are the "tightest" obstructions and will supply our lower bounds.

**Definition 2.3 (Exclusive subspace).** The boundary token's exclusive subspace at width $k$ is
modelled by a tuple $v = (v_1,\dots,v_k) \in V^{k}$, each entry drawn independently and uniformly
from $V$. One draw represents one exclusive dimension. The sample space is $V^{k}$, of size
$p^{nk}$, with counting measure normalised by $|V|^{k}$.

**Definition 2.4 (Obstructions).** The trained dynamics' degenerate directions are modelled by a
finite family $W_1,\dots,W_m$ of *proper* subspaces $W_j \subsetneq V$, $m \ge 1$.

**Definition 2.5 (Failure).** The tuple $v$ **fails** if some obstruction swallows it entirely:
$$\exists j \in \{1,\dots,m\} \ \ \forall i \in \{1,\dots,k\}: \ v_i \in W_j.$$
Write $N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) := \#\{v \in V^k : v \text{ fails}\}$,
$$P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) := \frac{N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)}{|V|^{k}}, \qquad
P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) := 1 - P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k).$$

**Interpretation.** The exclusive subspace is useful only if it is not entirely contained in a
direction along which the readout is blind. Containment of the *whole* span is the right failure
condition: a single surviving direction outside every obstruction is enough for a linear readout to
separate the boundary symbol. Note that this makes the model *maximally generous* to the naive
"one dimension suffices" hypothesis — and it still fails.

**Lemma 2.6 (Exact single-obstruction count).** For a fixed subspace $W \le V$,
$$\#\{v \in V^k : \forall i,\ v_i \in W\} = |W|^{k}.$$
*Proof.* The set of such tuples is in bijection with $W^k$ by restricting codomains. $\square$

---

## 3. The monotone-ramp theorem

### 3.1 Monotonicity

> **Theorem 3.1 (Prefix fibration).** For every $k$,
> $$N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k+1) \;\le\; N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)\cdot |V|.$$

*Proof sketch.* Map a failing $(k+1)$-tuple $v$ to the pair $\big((v_1,\dots,v_k),\, v_{k+1}\big)$.
The first component is again failing, since the obstruction $W_j$ witnessing the failure of $v$
contains all of $v_1,\dots,v_k$ in particular. The map is injective, because the pair determines $v$
coordinatewise. Its codomain has cardinality $N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)\cdot|V|$. $\square$

> **Theorem 3.2 (Monotone ramp).** $P_{\mathrm{fail}}$ is antitone and hence $P_{\mathrm{cure}}$ is
> monotone nondecreasing in $k$.

*Proof sketch.* Divide Theorem 3.1 by $|V|^{k+1}$:
$$P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k+1) = \frac{N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k+1)}{|V|^{k+1}}
\le \frac{N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)\,|V|}{|V|^{k+1}} = P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k).$$
Antitonicity for all pairs $k \le l$ follows from the successor step by induction. $\square$

This is the first empirical claim, now a theorem, and note how little it uses: no structure on the
obstruction family beyond being a family of subspaces (properness is not even needed here).

### 3.2 No capacity cliff

> **Theorem 3.3 (Strict positivity of failure).** If $m \ge 1$ then $N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) > 0$, hence
> $P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) > 0$ and $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) < 1$, for *every* finite width $k$.

*Proof.* The zero tuple $v_1 = \dots = v_k = 0$ lies in $W_1$ coordinatewise, since every subspace
contains $0$. $\square$

Trivial to prove, and decisive in consequence:

> **Corollary 3.4 (No cliff).** There is no $k_0$ such that $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) = 0$ for all
> $k < k_0$ and $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) = 1$ for all $k \ge k_0$. In particular the reliability curve
> is never a step function.

*Proof.* Such a $k_0$ would give $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k_0) = 1$, contradicting Theorem 3.3. $\square$

The empirical $100\%$ at $k = 4, 8$ is therefore a small-sample artefact under the model, not a
witnessed certainty; the model predicts that a sufficiently large replicate count at any fixed width
will exhibit failures.

### 3.3 Convergence to certainty

> **Theorem 3.5 (Union bound).** If every $W_j$ is proper then
> $$P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) \;\le\; \frac{m}{p^{k}}.$$

*Proof sketch.* Failing tuples inject into the disjoint union over $j$ of the tuples contained in
$W_j$, so $N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) \le \sum_{j} |W_j|^{k}$ by Lemma 2.6. By Lemma 2.2, $|W_j| \cdot p
\le |V|$, hence $|W_j|^k p^k \le |V|^k$ termwise. Summing over $j$ gives $N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)\,p^k
\le m |V|^k$, which is the claim after division. $\square$

**Definition 3.6 (Monotone ramp).** A reliability curve $P : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a
**monotone ramp** if (a) $P$ is monotone nondecreasing, (b) $P(k) < 1$ for all $k$, and (c)
$P(k) \to 1$ as $k \to \infty$.

> **Theorem 3.7 (Main law: the exclusive-width reliability curve is a monotone ramp).**
> For $m \ge 1$ obstructions, all proper, the curve $k \mapsto P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k)$ is a monotone
> ramp.

*Proof sketch.* (a) is Theorem 3.2, (b) is Theorem 3.3. For (c), squeeze:
$1 - m p^{-k} \le P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \le 1$ by Theorem 3.5, and $m p^{-k} \to 0$ because $p \ge 2$.
$\square$

> **Corollary 3.8 (No critical width).** A monotone ramp admits no width $k$ beyond which success is
> certain; yet for any $c < 1$ there is a width beyond which $P(l) > c$.

*Proof.* The first is (b); the second is (c) with the definition of convergence, plus monotonicity.
$\square$

Corollary 3.8 is the precise form of the phrase "no sharp width, but a real design rule": success is
never guaranteed, but any prescribed reliability level is reachable, at a width we now compute.

---

## 4. The two-sided envelope and the design rule

Theorem 3.5 bounds the failure mass from above. A matching lower bound needs one obstruction to be
as large as properness permits.

> **Lemma 4.1.** For each $j$, $|W_j|^{k} \le N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)$.

*Proof.* Tuples contained in $W_j$ are failing tuples; apply Lemma 2.6. $\square$

> **Theorem 4.2 (Hyperplane lower bound).** If some $W_j$ satisfies $|W_j|\cdot p = |V|$ (a
> hyperplane) then $P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) \ge p^{-k}$.

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 4.1, $N_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) \ge |W_j|^k = (|V|/p)^k$; divide by $|V|^k$.
$\square$

> **Theorem 4.3 (Two-sided geometric envelope).** With all $W_j$ proper and at least one a
> hyperplane,
> $$\frac{1}{p^{k}} \;\le\; 1 - P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \;\le\; \frac{m}{p^{k}} \qquad \text{for all } k.$$

The deficiency of the ramp is thus *exactly* of order $p^{-k}$: the two bounds have the same
geometric ratio and differ only by the constant $m$. This rules out both a super-geometric collapse
(a cliff) and a sub-geometric decay (a plateau).

> **Theorem 4.4 (Sufficient width).** If $m \le \epsilon\, p^{k}$ — i.e. $k \ge \log_p(m/\epsilon)$ —
> then $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \ge 1 - \epsilon$.

> **Theorem 4.5 (Necessary width).** If some obstruction is a hyperplane and
> $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \ge 1 - \epsilon$, then $p^{-k} \le \epsilon$, i.e.
> $k \ge \log_p(1/\epsilon)$.

*Proof sketches.* Immediate from Theorems 3.5 and 4.2 respectively, rearranged. $\square$

**The design rule.** The necessary and sufficient widths differ by the additive constant
$\log_p m$ — never by a multiplicative factor. Hence:

> The *location* of the reliability knee is determined to within $\log_p m$, even though the knee has
> no *sharpness* at all.

Calibrating to the data: at $p = 2$, a target of $\epsilon = 0.05$ needs $k \ge \log_2 20 \approx
4.3$ and is guaranteed by $k \ge \log_2(20 m)$. With $m$ in the range $8$–$16$ obstruction modes,
this reproduces the empirical prescription: **reserve at least four exclusive dimensions** for a
boundary token; two is near-robust; one is fragile.

---

## 5. The exact curve in the single-hyperplane case

Take $m = 1$ with the single obstruction $W$ a hyperplane, $|W|\cdot p = |V|$.

> **Theorem 5.1 (Exact curve).** $P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) = p^{-k}$ and hence
> $$P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) = 1 - p^{-k}.$$

*Proof sketch.* With one obstruction, failing tuples are exactly the tuples contained in $W$, of
which there are $|W|^k = (|V|/p)^k$ by Lemma 2.6. Divide by $|V|^k$. $\square$

> **Corollary 5.2 (Zero exclusive dimensions never work).** $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(0) = 0$.

> **Corollary 5.3 (The first exclusive dimension is not sufficient).**
> $$P_{\mathrm{cure}}(1) = 1 - \frac{1}{p} < 1.$$

This is the formal refutation of the "any exclusive dimension suffices" reading. Exclusivity is not
Boolean: the first private direction buys a fixed fraction $1 - 1/p$ of the reliability budget, and
the remainder must be bought dimension by dimension.

> **Theorem 5.4 (Strict monotonicity).** $k \mapsto P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k)$ is strictly increasing:
> every extra exclusive dimension strictly helps.

> **Theorem 5.5 (Sublinear benefit).** The marginal gain of the $(k+1)$-st exclusive dimension is
> $$P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k+1) - P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) = \frac{p-1}{p^{k+1}},$$
> and this quantity is strictly decreasing in $k$.

*Proof sketch.* Substitute Theorem 5.1 and simplify: $p^{-k} - p^{-(k+1)} = (p-1)p^{-(k+1)}$.
Strict decrease follows since $p > 1$. $\square$

Diminishing returns, quantitatively: the reliability gained per dimension is itself geometric.

> **Theorem 5.6 (Total failure mass).**
> $$\sum_{k \ge 0} P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) = \sum_{k \ge 0} p^{-k} = \frac{p}{p-1}.$$

This arithmetic invariant of the ramp is the seed of Section 7.

**A concrete witness.** The hypotheses are satisfiable: take $V = \mathbb{F}_p$ itself with the
single obstruction $W = \{0\}$, which is proper (since $\mathbb{F}_p$ is nontrivial) and of index
exactly $p$. Then the curve is literally $1 - p^{-k}$, and at $p = 2$ the widths used in the
experiment give

| $k$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| model $P_{\mathrm{cure}}$ | $0$ | $\tfrac12 = 0.5$ | $\tfrac34 = 0.75$ | $\tfrac{15}{16} = 0.9375$ | $\tfrac{255}{256} \approx 0.996$ |
| measured | $0.25$ | $0.33$ | $0.83$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ |

The agreement is qualitative and structural rather than numerical — the model is not fitted — but it
reproduces the ordering, the knee between $k=1$ and $k=4$, the sublinearity, and (crucially) the
prediction that the two measured $1.00$s are really $0.94$ and $0.996$ sampled six times each. The
probability of observing six consecutive successes at true rate $0.9375$ is $0.68$; at $0.996$ it is
$0.98$. Both observations are unsurprising under the ramp model.

---

## 6. Are the exclusive dimensions really exclusive? A $q$-Pochhammer bound

The model draws $k$ vectors and calls their span the token's $k$-dimensional exclusive subspace. If
the draws are dependent, the token has fewer private directions than advertised and the phrase "$k$
exclusive dimensions" overclaims. We quantify the risk.

**Definition 6.1.** Let $P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k) := \dfrac{\#\{v \in V^{k} : v_1,\dots,v_k \text{
linearly independent}\}}{|V|^{k}}$.

> **Theorem 6.2 ($q$-Pochhammer formula).** For $k \le n = \dim V$,
> $$P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k) = \prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1 - \frac{p^{i}}{p^{n}}\right).$$

*Proof sketch.* The classical count of linearly independent $k$-tuples over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with
$q = p$ is $\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}(p^{n} - p^{i})$: having chosen $i$ independent vectors, the $(i+1)$-st
must lie outside their span, a subspace of exactly $p^{i}$ elements. Factor $p^{n}$ out of each of
the $k$ terms and divide by $|V|^k = (p^n)^k$. $\square$

The product on the right is a truncated $q$-Pochhammer symbol $(p^{-n}; p)_k$ in disguise, the same
object that counts flags and subspaces over finite fields. To turn it into a usable bound we need an
elementary inequality.

> **Lemma 6.3 (Weierstrass product inequality).** If $0 \le a_i \le 1$ for $i < k$ then
> $$1 - \sum_{i<k} a_i \;\le\; \prod_{i<k}(1 - a_i).$$

*Proof sketch.* Induction on $k$. The base case is $1 \le 1$. For the step, write $S =
\sum_{i<k} a_i \ge 0$ and use the inductive hypothesis multiplied by the nonnegative factor
$1 - a_k$:
$$\prod_{i \le k}(1-a_i) \ge (1 - S)(1 - a_k) = 1 - S - a_k + S a_k \ge 1 - S - a_k,$$
the last step because $S a_k \ge 0$. $\square$

> **Theorem 6.4 (Genericity bound).** For $k \le n$,
> $$P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k) \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{p^{k} - 1}{(p-1)\,p^{n}}.$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply Lemma 6.3 to $a_i = p^{i}/p^{n}$ (each lies in $[0,1]$ because $i < k \le n$),
then sum the geometric series $\sum_{i<k} p^{i} = (p^{k}-1)/(p-1)$. $\square$

> **Theorem 6.5 (Genericity is antitone).** For $k + 1 \le n$, $P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k+1) \le
> P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k)$.

*Proof sketch.* The product for $k+1$ is that for $k$ times the factor $1 - p^{k-n} \le 1$, and the
product for $k$ is nonnegative. $\square$

So genericity *decays* in $k$, in the opposite direction to reliability. In the regime of the
experiment ($p = 2$, ambient hidden width $n = 192$, $k \le 8$) the genericity loss is at most
$(2^{8}-1)\cdot 2^{-192} \approx 2^{-184}$: utterly negligible, so the model of Sections 3–5 is not
vacuous and the reliability term alone governs. But the two effects genuinely compete, and combining
them is the point.

> **Theorem 6.6 (Reliability and genericity together).** For proper obstructions $W_1,\dots,W_m$ and
> $k \le n$, the probability that the drawn tuple is **both** linearly independent **and** escapes
> every obstruction satisfies
> $$\mathbb{P}\big(\text{independent} \wedge \text{cured}\big) \;\ge\;
> 1 - \frac{m}{p^{k}} - \frac{p^{k}-1}{(p-1)\,p^{n}}.$$

*Proof sketch.* Let $I$, $G$, $F$ be the sets of independent tuples, of independent-and-cured tuples,
and of failing tuples respectively. Then $I \subseteq G \cup F$, so $|I| \le |G| + |F|$; divide by
$|V|^k$ to get $P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k) \le \mathbb{P}(G) + P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k)$, and substitute the
lower bound of Theorem 6.4 and the upper bound of Theorem 3.5. $\square$

**The interior optimum.** Write the bound as $f(k) = 1 - m p^{-k} - (p^{k}-1)/((p-1)p^{n})$. The
first error term decays geometrically in $k$; the second grows geometrically in $k$. Their sum is
convex in $p^{k}$ and minimised in the interior, near
$$k^{*} \approx \tfrac12\Big(n + \log_p\big(m(p-1)\big)\Big),$$
i.e. roughly half the ambient width, with maximum value $1 - \Theta(p^{-n/2})$. This is the
structural reason the reliability curve cannot be a cliff: a cliff is what one monotone force
produces; here two opposed forces act, and the resulting optimum is a smooth interior maximum, not an
edge.

---

## 7. The Euler-product bridge

Theorem 5.6 computed the total failure mass at characteristic $p$ as $\sum_{k\ge 0} p^{-k} =
(1 - p^{-1})^{-1}$. That is the local Euler factor of the Riemann zeta function at $p$. The
coincidence is not accidental — the model *is* a geometric distribution over widths with ratio
$1/p$ — but it becomes a genuine cross-domain identity once we let the characteristic vary.

**Definition 7.1 (Damped failure-mass series).** For $s \in \mathbb{C}$, weight a width-$k$ failure
by $p^{-ks}$ rather than $p^{-k}$, and set
$$Z_p(s) := \sum_{k \ge 0} \left(p^{-s}\right)^{k}.$$

> **Lemma 7.2.** For $p \ge 2$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ we have $|p^{-s}| = p^{-\operatorname{Re}
> s} < 1$.

> **Theorem 7.3 (Local factor).** For $p \ge 2$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
> $$Z_p(s) = \left(1 - p^{-s}\right)^{-1}.$$

*Proof.* Geometric series, convergent by Lemma 7.2. $\square$

> **Theorem 7.4 (The $s = 1$ case, from the model).** In the single-hyperplane model over
> $\mathbb{F}_p$, the total failure mass of the reliability ramp is
> $$\sum_{k \ge 0} P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) = \left(1 - p^{-1}\right)^{-1}.$$

This is computed from the model — via the exact curve of Theorem 5.1 — rather than postulated.

> **Theorem 7.5 (Bridge).** For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
> $$\prod_{p \text{ prime}} Z_p(s) \;=\; \zeta(s).$$

*Proof sketch.* Substitute Theorem 7.3 factorwise and invoke the Euler product for $\zeta$. $\square$

> **Corollary 7.6 (Closed form at $s = 2$).**
> $$\prod_{p \text{ prime}} Z_p(2) \;=\; \zeta(2) \;=\; \frac{\pi^{2}}{6}.$$

**What this means, and what it doesn't.** The left-hand side is assembled purely from the
finite-field reliability model; the right-hand side is the analytic zeta function. No claim is being
made that number theory governs neural networks. The content is structural: the ramp's failure
spectrum, as a function of width, has exactly the shape of a local Euler factor, and the aggregate
over characteristics is $\zeta$. And it carries a moral about the cliff/ramp dichotomy that is
sharper than any of the finite statements above:

> An Euler factor exists because the local series is *infinite*. A capacity cliff would make the
> failure mass a finite sum, collapsing the factor to a polynomial and destroying the identity. The
> zeta bridge holds precisely because the ramp never terminates.

---

## 8. Algorithms and numerics

Everything above is computable, and the computations are useful for calibration.

**Algorithm A (Exact multi-obstruction failure probability by inclusion–exclusion).** Given the
codimensions of all intersections $\bigcap_{j \in S} W_j$ over nonempty $S \subseteq \{1,\dots,m\}$,
$$P_{\mathrm{fail}}(k) = \sum_{\emptyset \ne S \subseteq \{1,\dots,m\}} (-1)^{|S|+1}\,
p^{-k\,\mathrm{codim}\left(\bigcap_{j \in S} W_j\right)},$$
because the tuples contained in a subspace $U$ number $|U|^k = p^{-k\,\mathrm{codim}\,U}|V|^k$ and
inclusion–exclusion over the lattice generated by the obstructions is exact. Cost: $O(2^{m})$ terms,
each a single power. This refines the union bound of Theorem 3.5 to an identity, and exhibits
$P_{\mathrm{fail}}$ as a finite Dirichlet polynomial in $p^{-k}$ whose leading term is
$p^{-k\,\mathrm{codim}}$ for the minimal codimension present.

**Algorithm B (Knee localisation).** Given $p$, $m$, and a tolerance $\epsilon$, return the pair
$\big(\lceil \log_p(1/\epsilon)\rceil,\ \lceil\log_p(m/\epsilon)\rceil\big)$ of necessary and
sufficient widths (Theorems 4.4–4.5). Constant cost; the output is a bracketing interval of length
$\lceil \log_p m\rceil$ that always contains the true minimal width.

**Algorithm C (Genericity product).** Evaluate $\prod_{i<k}(1 - p^{i-n})$ exactly in rational
arithmetic and compare against the closed-form bound $1 - (p^k-1)/((p-1)p^n)$; $O(k)$ multiplications.
Used to certify that the drawn directions really are $k$-dimensional.

**Algorithm D (Joint optimum search).** Maximise $f(k) = 1 - m p^{-k} - (p^{k}-1)/((p-1)p^{n})$ over
$0 \le k \le n$ by direct evaluation ($O(n)$) or by rounding the analytic optimum $k^{*} \approx
\frac12(n + \log_p(m(p-1)))$ and checking its two neighbours ($O(1)$).

**Algorithm E (Euler-product truncation).** Evaluate $\prod_{p \le X}(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$ over primes
up to $X$ by sieving and compare against $\zeta(s)$; the tail error is $O(X^{1-\operatorname{Re}s})$,
so convergence is fast for $s = 2$ and visibly slow near $s = 1$ — a numerical rendering of the fact
that the total failure mass at $s = 1$ diverges when aggregated over characteristics.

**Sampling check.** One can also verify the exact curves by Monte Carlo: draw $k$-tuples uniformly
from $\mathbb{F}_p^{n}$ and test containment in a fixed hyperplane $\{x : \langle a, x\rangle = 0\}$.
The empirical failure rate converges to $p^{-k}$, and the empirical independence rate to the
$q$-Pochhammer product, both at the usual $O(N^{-1/2})$ rate.

---

## 9. Discussion

### 9.1 What the model explains

Every qualitative feature of the measured table has a counterpart theorem.

| Empirical observation | Theorem |
|---|---|
| More exclusive width never hurts | Monotone ramp (Thm 3.2) |
| Widths $4$, $8$ show no failures | Strict positivity (Thm 3.3): a finite-sample effect |
| No sharp critical width | No cliff (Cor. 3.4), interior optimum (§6) |
| One exclusive dimension is not sufficient | $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(1) = 1 - 1/p$ (Cor. 5.3) |
| Benefit is sublinear | Marginal gain $(p-1)p^{-(k+1)}$, strictly decreasing (Thm 5.5) |
| Same failure mechanism at every width | Width enters only through the exponent $k$; the obstruction family is width-independent |
| "Reserve $\ge 4$ exclusive dimensions" | Design rule (Thms 4.4–4.5) with $p=2$, $m \approx 8$–$16$ |

### 9.2 What the model does not claim

The obstruction model is a *caricature*: it replaces a trained nonlinear recurrence by a fixed finite
family of linear degeneracies and replaces optimisation randomness by uniform sampling. It predicts
the *shape* of the reliability curve, not its numerical values; the fitted correspondence between the
model's $p, m$ and any particular architecture is not established here. In particular the empirical
$k=0$ value of $0.25$ exceeds the model's $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(0) = 0$, which is expected: with no
exclusive dimensions a real system can still succeed by other means (a fortunate shared-subspace
configuration), whereas the model's width-$0$ tuple is vacuously contained in every obstruction.

The statistical caveats of the underlying measurement should also be carried forward honestly: six
replicates per width make the $k{=}1 \to k{=}2$ jump alone insignificant (Fisher $\approx 0.24$); the
empirical case rests on the monotone ordering across four widths together with much larger merged
anchor samples at the extreme widths. Intermediate widths $k = 3$ and $k = 5$–$7$ remain untested, so
the exact location of the knee inside $(1,4)$ is empirically open — though the model brackets it to
within $\log_p m$.

### 9.3 Future directions

Three conjectures crystallise the open problems.

**C1. Exact multi-obstruction curve via subspace Möbius inversion.** The inclusion–exclusion identity
of Algorithm A should be established as a theorem, yielding in particular that $k \mapsto
P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k)$ is *strictly* increasing whenever $m \ge 1$ — closing the gap between the proved
antitonicity of $P_{\mathrm{fail}}$ and strict monotonicity, currently proved only for $m = 1$. The
key insight is that inclusion–exclusion over the lattice generated by the obstructions turns the
failure count into a signed sum of exact subspace counts, each already a power of $p$, so the entire
curve is a finite Dirichlet polynomial in $p^{-k}$ whose leading term forces strict decrease of the
failure mass. The exact single-subspace count and the union bound are already in hand; only the
alternating-sum bookkeeping and the Gaussian-binomial computation of intersection codimensions
remain.

**C2. The knee is at $k = \lceil \log_p m \rceil$.** Define the knee $k^{*}(m,p) := \min\{k :
1 - P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \le 1/2\}$. We conjecture $\lceil\log_p m\rceil \le k^{*}(m,p) \le
\lceil\log_p(2m)\rceil$, so that the empirical "reserve $\ge 4$ exclusive dimensions" rule is exactly
the statement that the system has $m \approx 8$–$16$ obstruction modes at $p = 2$. The two-sided
envelope of Theorem 4.3 already pins the deficiency between $p^{-k}$ and $mp^{-k}$, so the knee can
move only by an additive $\log_p m$, never by a multiplicative factor: a threshold *location* result
in the absence of threshold *sharpness*. What remains is a monotone-inversion lemma for
$k \mapsto m p^{-k}$.

**C3. The ramp/anti-ramp trade-off has an interior optimum.** The lower bound $f(k) = 1 - mp^{-k} -
(p^{k}-1)/((p-1)p^{n})$ of Theorem 6.6 should be maximised at $k^{*} = \lfloor (n + \log_p(m(p-1)))/2
\rfloor + O(1)$ — the best exclusive width is roughly $n/2$ — with maximum value $1 - \Theta(p^{-n/2})$.
The reliability error decays like $p^{-k}$ while the genericity error grows like $p^{k-n}$, so the
sum is a convex Laurent-type expression in $p^{k}$ with an explicit minimiser.

Beyond these: a mechanistic reading of the $k = 1$ case (measuring the boundary token's exclusive
coordinate at cure versus at failure), and transfer of the exclusive-dimension design rule to
full-scale systems with a genuine exclusive-dimension boundary input.

### 9.4 Methodological coda

The broadest lesson is about how thresholds are inferred. At any width where the true failure
probability is, say, $0.2$, five out of six replicates look like a clean success — and a
single-replicate study looks like a discovered threshold. Ramps masquerade as cliffs routinely. The
remedy is not more precise measurement at one width but measurement across several widths against a
model that says what the alternatives look like. The theorems above supply exactly that: a family of
curves in which monotonicity, the insufficiency of the first dimension, diminishing returns, geometric
approach to certainty, and the strict impossibility of attaining it are all consequences of one
elementary counting argument.

---

## 10. Summary of results

1. **Monotone ramp.** $k \mapsto P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k)$ is nondecreasing (prefix fibration), strictly
   below $1$ for every finite $k$ (zero tuple), and converges to $1$ (union bound).
2. **No capacity cliff.** The reliability curve is never a step function; no finite exclusive width
   certifies success.
3. **Two-sided geometric envelope.** $p^{-k} \le 1 - P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) \le m p^{-k}$, hence
   necessary width $\log_p(1/\epsilon)$ and sufficient width $\log_p(m/\epsilon)$ for reliability
   $1-\epsilon$: the knee is located to within $\log_p m$.
4. **Exact hyperplane curve.** $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(k) = 1 - p^{-k}$, so $P_{\mathrm{cure}}(1) =
   1 - 1/p$ — the first exclusive dimension is not sufficient — and the marginal gain
   $(p-1)p^{-(k+1)}$ strictly decreases. At $p = 2$ the predicted values at the tested widths are
   $0, \tfrac12, \tfrac34, \tfrac{15}{16}, \tfrac{255}{256}$.
5. **$q$-Pochhammer genericity.** $P_{\mathrm{ind}}(k) = \prod_{i<k}(1 - p^{i-n}) \ge
   1 - (p^{k}-1)/((p-1)p^{n})$, decreasing in $k$; the model's exclusive dimensions are genuinely
   exclusive in the experimental regime.
6. **Interior optimum.** $\mathbb{P}(\text{independent} \wedge \text{cured}) \ge 1 - mp^{-k} -
   (p^{k}-1)/((p-1)p^{n})$, a two-sided window whose error terms move oppositely in $k$.
7. **Euler bridge.** The ramp's total failure mass at characteristic $p$ is $(1-p^{-1})^{-1}$; the
   width-damped masses multiply over all characteristics to $\zeta(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$,
   and to $\pi^{2}/6$ at $s = 2$.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Callable, Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Brute-force ground truth over small finite vector spaces
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def all_vectors(p: int, n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Enumerate every vector of F_p^n as a tuple of residues."""
    return itertools.product(range(p), repeat=n)


def in_kernel(v: Sequence[int], functionals: Sequence[Sequence[int]], p: int) -> bool:
    """True iff v lies in the common kernel of the given linear functionals over F_p."""
    for a in functionals:
        if sum(ai * vi for ai, vi in zip(a, v)) % p != 0:
            return False
    return True


def brute_force_fail_prob(
    p: int, n: int, obstructions: Sequence[Sequence[Sequence[int]]], k: int
) -> Fraction:
    """
    Exact P_fail(k) by full enumeration of V^k.

    Each obstruction is given as a list of linear functionals (rows); the obstruction
    subspace is their common kernel.  A tuple fails iff some obstruction contains all
    of its k entries.
    """
    vectors: List[Tuple[int, ...]] = list(all_vectors(p, n))
    # Precompute, for each obstruction, the set of vectors it contains.
    members: List[set] = [
        {v for v in vectors if in_kernel(v, obs, p)} for obs in obstructions
    ]
    total = 0
    failing = 0
    for tup in itertools.product(vectors, repeat=k):
        total += 1
        if any(all(v in mem for v in tup) for mem in members):
            failing += 1
    return Fraction(failing, total)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Closed-form curves
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------


def hyperplane_cure_prob(p: int, k: int) -> Fraction:
    """Exact reliability of the single-hyperplane model: 1 - p^{-k}."""
    return Fraction(1) - Fraction(1, p**k)


def marginal_gain(p: int, k: int) -> Fraction:
    """Reliability bought by the (k+1)-st exclusive dimension: (p-1)/p^{k+1}."""
    return Fraction(p - 1, p ** (k + 1))


def envelope(p: int, m: int, k: int) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:

algorithms.name: Exact Multi-Obstruction Failure Probability by Subspace Mobius Inversion
algorithms.description: Computes the failure probability of the exclusive-dimension model exactly, without the slack of the union bound, for an arbitrary family of obstruction subspaces. Since the k-tuples contained in a subspace U number |U|^k = p^{-k codim U} |V|^k, inclusion-exclusion over the lattice generated by the obstructions gives P_fail(k) = sum over nonempty S of (-1)^{|S|+1} p^{-k codim(intersection over S)}. This exhibits the whole reliability curve as a finite Dirichlet polynomial in p^{-k}, whose leading term is governed by the smallest codimension present, and whose alternating structure is the route to strict monotonicity for m > 1. Complexity: O(2^m) rational terms for the probability, plus O(2^m * m * n^2) field operations to build the codimension table by Gaussian elimination over F_p. All arithmetic is exact.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: prime p, width k, obstruction hyperplane functionals a_1..a_m in F_p^n
OUTPUT: exact rational P_fail(k)

1. FOR each nonempty S subset of {1..m}:
2.     M <- matrix whose rows are the functionals a_j for j in S
3.     codim[S] <- rank of M over F_p            # Gaussian elimination mod p
4. total <- 0
5. FOR each nonempty S subset of {1..m}:
6.     sign <- +1 if |S| is odd else -1
7.     total <- total + sign * p^{-k * codim[S]} # exact rational arithmetic
8. RETURN total

CORRECTNESS: the failing tuples are the union over j of the tuples inside W_j; the tuples
inside the intersection over S number p^{-k codim} |V|^k exactly, and inclusion-exclusion
over a finite union of these sets is exact.

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, List, Sequence, Tuple


def failure_probability_inclusion_exclusion(
    p: int, k: int, codimension: Dict[FrozenSet[int], int]
) -> Fraction:
    """
    Exact failure probability of the exclusive-dimension model with m obstruction
    subspaces, by Moebius inversion over the lattice they generate.

        P_fail(k) = sum over nonempty S of (-1)^{|S|+1} p^{-k * codim(inter_{j in S} W_j)}

    `codimension` maps each nonempty subset S of obstruction indices to the codimension
    of the intersection of the corresponding subspaces.  Exact rational arithmetic.
    """
    total = Fraction(0)
    for subset, codim in codimension.items():
        if not subset:
            continue
        sign = 1 if len(subset) % 2 == 1 else -1
        total += sign * Fraction(1, p ** (k * codim))
    return total


def codimensions_from_functionals(
    p: int, n: int, functionals: Sequence[Sequence[int]]
) -> Dict[FrozenSet[int], int]:
    """
    Build the codimension table for m hyperplanes given as kernels of single linear
    functionals over F_p: codim of an intersection is the rank of the stacked rows,
    computed by Gaussian elimination over F_p.
    """

    def rank_mod_p(rows: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        rows = [r[:] for r in rows]
        rank, pivot_col = 0, 0
        while rank < len(rows) and pivot_col < n:
            pivot = None
            for r in range(rank, len(rows)):
                if rows[r][pivot_col] % p != 0:
                    pivot = r
                    break
            if pivot is None:
                pivot_col += 1
                continue
            rows[rank], rows[pivot] = rows[pivot], rows[rank]
            inv = pow(rows[rank][pivot_col], p - 2, p)
            rows[rank] = [(x * inv) % p for x in rows[rank]]
            for r in range(len(rows)):
                if r != rank and rows[r][pivot_col] % p != 0:
                    f = rows[r][pivot_col]
                    rows[r] = [(a - f * b) % p for a, b in zip(rows[r], rows[rank])]
            rank += 1
            pivot_col += 1
        return rank

    m = len(functionals)
    table: Dict[FrozenSet[int], int] = {}
    for size in range(1, m + 1):
        for subset in itertools.combinations(range(m), size):
            table[frozenset(subset)] = rank_mod_p([list(functionals[j]) for j in subset])
    return table

The hyperplane lower bound p^{-k} <= eps forces k >= log_p(1/eps); the union bound m p^{-k} <= eps guarantees reliability 1 - eps once k >= log_p(m/eps). Since the two differ by the additive constant log_p m and never by a multiplicative factor, the knee of the reliability curve is *located* to within ceil(log_p m) even though the curve has no sharp threshold whatsoever. 2. k_necessary  <- ceil( log_p (1 / eps) )     # from p^{-k} <= 1 - P_cure
3. k_sufficient <- ceil( log_p (m / eps) )     # from 1 - P_cure <= m p^{-k}
4. k_sufficient <- max(k_necessary, k_sufficient)

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Tuple


def knee_bracket(p: int, m: int, eps: float) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """
    Bracket the minimal exclusive width achieving reliability 1 - eps.

    Necessary : k >= log_p(1/eps)     (hyperplane lower bound p^{-k} <= eps)
    Sufficient: k >= log_p(m/eps)     (union bound m p^{-k} <= eps)

    The bracket has width ceil(log_p m): the knee is LOCATED even though the
    reliability curve has no sharp threshold.  O(1) time.
    """
    if not (0.0 < eps < 1.0):
        raise ValueError("eps must lie strictly between 0 and 1")
    necessary = math.ceil(math.log(1.0 / eps, p))
    sufficient = math.ceil(math.log(m / eps, p))
    return necessary, max(necessary, sufficient)

algorithms.name: q-Pochhammer Genericity Certificate for the Drawn Exclusive Directions
algorithms.description: Certifies that the k randomly drawn directions really do span a k-dimensional subspace, so that the phrase 'k exclusive dimensions' is honest. The exact probability is the truncated q-Pochhammer product over i < k of (1 - p^{i-n}), obtained from the classical count product over i < k of (p^n - p^i) of linearly independent tuples: having chosen i independent vectors, the next must avoid their span, a subspace of exactly p^i elements. The routine returns both the exact rational value and the closed-form Weierstrass lower bound 1 - (p^k - 1)/((p-1) p^n), which is provably valid and far cheaper to reason about. Complexity: O(k) multiplications of integers of O(n log p) bits.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: prime p, ambient dimension n, width k <= n
OUTPUT: (P_ind exact, closed-form lower bound)

1. exact <- 1
2. FOR i = 0 .. k-1:
3.     exact <- exact * (1 - p^i / p^n)        # exact rational arithmetic
4. bound <- 1 - (p^k - 1) / ((p - 1) * p^n)    # Weierstrass + geometric series
5. ASSERT bound <= exact
6. RETURN (exact, bound)

CORRECTNESS: 1 - sum a_i <= prod (1 - a_i) for a_i in [0,1] with a_i = p^{i-n}, and
sum over i < k of p^i = (p^k - 1)/(p - 1).

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Tuple


def genericity_certificate(p: int, n: int, k: int) -> Tuple[Fraction, Fraction]:
    """
    Return (exact q-Pochhammer genericity probability, closed-form lower bound):

        P_ind(k) = prod_{i<k} (1 - p^{i-n})   >=   1 - (p^k - 1)/((p-1) p^n).

    Exact rational arithmetic, O(k) multiplications of O(n log p)-bit integers.
    """
    if k > n:
        raise ValueError("k must not exceed the ambient dimension n")
    exact = Fraction(1)
    for i in range(k):
        exact *= Fraction(1) - Fraction(p**i, p**n)
    bound = Fraction(1) - Fraction(p**k - 1, (p - 1) * p**n)
    return exact, bound

algorithms.name: Interior Optimum of the Reliability-Genericity Trade-Off
algorithms.description: Maximises the joint lower bound f(k) = 1 - m p^{-k} - (p^k - 1)/((p-1) p^n) on the probability that the boundary token both occupies a genuinely k-dimensional exclusive subspace and escapes every obstruction. The first error term decays geometrically in k (more private directions are harder for an obstruction to swallow) while the second grows geometrically in k (more draws are likelier to collide), so the objective is convex in p^k and its maximiser is strictly interior, near k* = (n + log_p(m(p-1)))/2. The routine evaluates a small window around the analytic estimate and falls back to an exhaustive O(n) scan if the maximiser lies outside it; all comparisons are exact rational. This interior optimum is the structural reason a reliability cliff is impossible: a cliff is what a single monotone force produces.
algorithms.pseudocode:
INPUT: prime p, ambient dimension n, obstruction count m
OUTPUT: (k*, f(k*)) maximising the joint reliability-and-genericity bound

1. DEFINE f(k) = 1 - m p^{-k} - (p^k - 1) / ((p-1) p^n)      # exact rational
2. guess <- round( (n + log_p (m (p-1))) / 2 )
3. window <- [max(0, guess-4) .. min(n, guess+4)]
4. k* <- argmax over window of f
5. IF k* is an endpoint of window THEN k* <- argmax over 0..n of f
6. RETURN (k*, f(k*))

COMPLEXITY: O(1) evaluations typically, O(n) in the fallback; each evaluation costs
O(n log p)-bit rational arithmetic.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Tuple


def optimal_exclusive_width(p: int, n: int, m: int) -> Tuple[int, Fraction]:
    """
    Maximise the joint reliability-and-genericity lower bound

        f(k) = 1 - m p^{-k} - (p^k - 1)/((p-1) p^n),   0 <= k <= n,

    whose two error terms move in opposite directions in k.  Uses the analytic
    estimate k* ~ (n + log_p(m(p-1)))/2 and verifies a small window around it,
    falling back to O(n) exhaustive search; exact rational comparisons throughout.
    """

    def f(k: int) -> Fraction:
        return (
            Fraction(1)
            - Fraction(m, p**k)
            - Fraction(p**k - 1, (p - 1) * p**n)
        )

    guess = int(round(0.5 * (n + math.log(m * (p - 1), p))))
    window = [k for k in range(max(0, guess - 4), min(n, guess + 4) + 1)]
    best = max(window, key=f)
    if best in (window[0], window[-1]):  # boundary hit: full search
        best = max(range(n + 1), key=f)
    return best, f(best)

Run: python viz_tradeoff.py   (writes tradeoff_and_zeta.png)
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def primes_up_to(limit: int) -> List[int]:
    sieve = [True] * (limit + 1)
    sieve[0:2] = [False, False]
    for i in range(2, int(limit**0.5) + 1):
        if sieve[i]:
            for j in range(i * i, limit + 1, i):
                sieve[j] = False
    return [i for i, ok in enumerate(sieve) if ok]


def euler_product(s: float, limit: int) -> float:
    prod = 1.0
    for p in primes_up_to(limit):
        prod *= 1.0 / (1.0 - p ** (-s))
    return prod


def main() -> None:
    p, n, m = 2, 24, 8
    ks = np.arange(0, n + 1)
    reliability_err = m * float(p) ** (-ks.astype(float))
    genericity_err = (float(p) ** ks.astype(float) - 1.0) / ((p - 1) * float(p) ** n)
    total = reliability_err + genericity_err
    kstar = int(np.argmin(total))

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.2))

    ax1.semilogy(ks, reliability_err, "o-", color="#1f77b4", lw=2,
                 label=r"reliability error $m\,p^{-k}$")
    ax1.semilogy(ks, genericity_err + 1e-300, "s-", color="#2ca02c", lw=2,
                 label=r"genericity error $(p^k-1)/((p-1)p^n)$")
    ax1.semilogy(ks, total, "k-", lw=2.4, label="total error")
    ax1.axvline(kstar, color="crimson", ls="--", lw=1.6,
                label=fr"interior optimum $k^*={kstar}\approx n/2$")
    ax1.set_xlabel("exclusive dimensions $k$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("error (log scale)")
    ax1.set_title(f"Two opposed geometric forces  ($p={p}$, $n={n}$, $m={m}$)")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3, which="both")
    ax1.legend(fontsize=9)

    xs = [10, 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000]
    for s, target, colour, name in [
        (2.0, math.pi**2 / 6, "#1f77b4", r"$\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6$"),
        (3.0, 1.2020569031595943, "#2ca02c", r"$\zeta(3)$"),
        (4.0, math.pi**4 / 90, "#9467bd", r"$\zeta(4)=\pi^4/90$"),
    ]:
        errs = [abs(euler_product(s, X) - target) for X in xs]
        ax2.loglog(xs, errs, "o-", color=colour, lw=2, label=f"s = {s:.0f},  {name}")

From Failure Masses to the Zeta Function

In the clean model the failure probability at exclusive width k is exactly p−k. Summing over all widths, with each width damped by an exponent s, gives the local factor Zp(s) = ∑k≥0 p−ks = (1 − p−s)−1. Multiply these across every characteristic and you obtain the Riemann zeta function ζ(s). Flip the cliff switch to truncate every ramp at a finite width — the Euler factors collapse and the identity dies. The bridge exists because the ramp never ends.

# How much private space does a full stop need? Teaching a machine to *stop* sounds like the easiest job in the pipeline. It isn't. Train the same sequence model five times with five random initialisations and you can get five different halting behaviours: some copies stop flawlessly on inputs longer than anything they were trained on, some trail off into gibberish, some stop *almost* always — and then don't, on the one long input you cared about. The folk explanation is that the boundary symbol needs **room**: coordinates in the representation space that nothing else uses. Its own *exclusive dimensions*. And the folk corollary is that **one** exclusive dimension ought to be enough — if there's a coordinate only the boundary symbol touches, a linear readout can find it. This page is about why that corollary is false, and about the exact shape of the truth. By the end you will have derived, played with, and numerically verified a small theory: the reliability of a boundary symbol as a function of its exclusive width is a **monotone ramp** — never decreasing, never reaching certainty, climbing at exactly geometric rate — and, in a twist nobody ordered, its failure spectrum is a local factor of the Riemann zeta function. --- ## 1. The measurement that started it Fix a recurrent model completely: architecture, data, training schedule, everything. Let one number vary — $E$, the number of coordinates the boundary token's learned representation may occupy, with the rest zero-padded. Write $k$ for the resulting count of *exclusive* dimensions. Train six fresh replicates at each width and ask one yes/no question of each: does it halt correctly, with confidence $\ge 0.99$, on inputs longer than any it saw in training? Call such a replicate **cured**. | exclusive dimensions $k$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fraction cured | $0.25$ | $0.33$ | $0.83$ | $1.00$ | $1.00$ | | worst replicate | $0.005$ | $0.157$ | $0.948$ | $1.000$ | $1.000$ | Read the $k=1$ row slowly. Two of six replicates were *perfect*; one scored $0.157$ — a hard failure. Same width, same architecture, same data, different seed. Whatever exclusivity buys, it is not a guarantee.
Why "cliff versus ramp" is the whole question A **cliff** model says: below a critical width the mechanism is impossible, at or above it guaranteed. A **ramp** model says: each extra exclusive dimension multiplies the failure rate by a constant factor less than one, and no finite width eliminates failure. They recommend different engineering (a hard budget versus a risk calculation), they predict different sampling behaviour (deterministic versus binomial), and they license very different conclusions from single-seed experiments. Six replicates per width cannot separate them — the $k{=}1 \to k{=}2$ jump alone is not statistically significant. What *can* separate them is a model that says what the alternatives look like. That's what we build next.
--- ## 2. A model you can actually compute with Reliability failures of this kind are **alignment** failures: the boundary token's private subspace lines up with a degenerate direction of the trained dynamics, one along which the readout simply cannot tell "stop" from "continue". Abstract away the mechanism and keep the geometry. > **The model.** Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n$ over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$. > The boundary token's exclusive subspace at width $k$ is generated by $k$ vectors > $v_1,\dots,v_k$ drawn independently and uniformly from $V$ — one draw per exclusive dimension. The > trained dynamics' degeneracies are a finite family of **proper** subspaces > $W_1,\dots,W_m \subsetneq V$. A run **fails** when some $W_j$ swallows the *whole* exclusive > subspace: $\exists j\ \forall i,\ v_i \in W_j$. Everything is now finite, so "probability" means counting: $$P_{\text{fail}}(k) = \frac{\#\{\text{failing } k\text{-tuples}\}}{|V|^{k}}, \qquad P_{\text{cure}}(k) = 1 - P_{\text{fail}}(k).$$ Note how generous this is to the folk hypothesis: a *single* surviving direction outside every obstruction already counts as success. And it still won't be enough. --- ## 3. Play with the ramp before you prove anything The widget below *is* the theory. Drag $p$ (how coarse the field is), $m$ (how many degenerate modes the system has), $n$ (the ambient width), and $k$ (the exclusive width you're buying). Three things to try: 1. Push $k$ high and watch the blue curve approach — but never touch — the dotted certainty line. 2. Compare the blue ramp against the dashed red "capacity cliff". Nothing you can do to the sliders makes the ramp look like the cliff. 3. Hit **Roll six seeds** at $k = 4$, repeatedly. You will see 6/6 cured most of the time, at a width whose true reliability is only $0.94$. That is exactly how a ramp counterfeits a threshold. {{interactive_demo:0}} --- ## 4. The four theorems, one at a time ### 4.1 Monotone: extra room never hurts > **Theorem.** $P_{\text{cure}}(k)$ is nondecreasing in $k$.
Click to reveal the proof — it's one sentence and a bijection Take any failing tuple of width $k+1$ and delete its last vector. What remains is a failing tuple of width $k$: the obstruction that swallowed everything still contains the survivors. The map $v \mapsto \big((v_1,\dots,v_k),\, v_{k+1}\big)$ is injective, so $$N_{\text{fail}}(k+1) \le N_{\text{fail}}(k) \cdot |V|.$$ Divide by $|V|^{k+1}$: the failure *probability* cannot increase. $\blacksquare$ Notice how little the argument uses. No structure on the obstructions beyond being subspaces, no properness, no independence. Monotonicity is essentially free.
### 4.2 Never certain: there is no capacity cliff > **Theorem.** For every finite $k$, $P_{\text{fail}}(k) > 0$; hence $P_{\text{cure}}(k) < 1$ always, > and the reliability curve is never a step function.
Click to reveal the proof — the witness is the zero vector Every subspace contains $0$. So the draw $v_1 = \dots = v_k = 0$ fails at every width, forever. There is always failing mass, hence never certainty. And a step function would require $P_{\text{cure}}(k_0) = 1$ at its jump, which cannot happen. $\blacksquare$ Consequence for the data: the measured $100\%$ at $k = 4$ and $k = 8$ *must* be a finite-sample effect under the model. Enough replicates would eventually turn up a failure.
### 4.3 Geometric: the ramp is pinned between two exponentials > **Theorem.** If all obstructions are proper and at least one is a hyperplane (index exactly $p$), > then for every $k$ > $$\frac{1}{p^{k}} \;\le\; 1 - P_{\text{cure}}(k) \;\le\; \frac{m}{p^{k}}.$$
Click to reveal both bounds *Upper (union bound).* A proper subspace has index at least $p$, so it contains at most $|V|/p$ vectors; the chance that all $k$ independent draws land inside one fixed obstruction is at most $p^{-k}$. Sum over the $m$ obstructions. *Lower.* If $W_j$ has index exactly $p$ then the tuples inside it number exactly $(|V|/p)^k$, and every one of them fails. So $P_{\text{fail}}(k) \ge p^{-k}$. $\blacksquare$ Both bounds have the *same* geometric ratio $1/p$ and differ only by the constant $m$. That rules out a super-geometric collapse (a cliff) and a sub-geometric decay (a plateau) simultaneously.
### 4.4 Exact, and sublinear With a single hyperplane obstruction the curve is exact: $$P_{\text{cure}}(k) = 1 - p^{-k}.$$ Two immediate corollaries. First, $P_{\text{cure}}(0) = 0$: no exclusive room, no reliability. Second — the punchline — $$P_{\text{cure}}(1) = 1 - \frac{1}{p} \;<\; 1: \qquad \textbf{the first exclusive dimension is not sufficient.}$$ And the marginal value of the $(k+1)$-st dimension is exactly $(p-1)/p^{k+1}$, strictly decreasing: diminishing returns, quantified. At $p = 2$ the curve reads $0,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac34,\ \tfrac{15}{16}, \ \tfrac{255}{256}$ at the tested widths $0,1,2,4,8$ — the same shape, the same knee, and the honest prediction that the two measured $1.00$s are really $0.94$ and $0.996$ sampled six times each. {{visualization:0}} --- ## 5. The design rule: a located knee without a sharp one Rearranging the two bounds of §4.3 gives a matched pair. - **Necessary:** reliability $1-\epsilon$ forces $k \ge \log_p(1/\epsilon)$. - **Sufficient:** $k \ge \log_p(m/\epsilon)$ guarantees reliability $1-\epsilon$. They differ by the *additive* constant $\log_p m$ — never by a multiplicative factor. So the knee's **location** is pinned even though the knee has no **sharpness** at all. Calibrated at $p = 2$ with $m$ around $8$–$16$ degenerate modes, this reproduces the empirical prescription: > **Reserve at least four exclusive dimensions for a boundary token.** Two is near-robust; one is a > coin flip dressed up as a design. The algorithm that computes the bracket is trivial and worth having on hand: {{algorithm:1}} For the exact curve with several obstructions — no union bound, no slack — inclusion–exclusion over the lattice they generate does the job, and exhibits the failure probability as a finite Dirichlet polynomial in $p^{-k}$: {{algorithm:0}} --- ## 6. Are the "exclusive" dimensions actually exclusive? A subtlety the phrase hides: we drew $k$ random vectors and called their span $k$-dimensional. Random vectors can be dependent. Does the model quietly overclaim? > **Theorem ($q$-Pochhammer genericity).** The probability that $k$ uniform draws from an > $n$-dimensional space over $\mathbb{F}_p$ are linearly independent is exactly > $$\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1 - \frac{p^{i}}{p^{n}}\right) \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{p^{k}-1}{(p-1)p^{n}}.$$
Click to reveal the counting argument and the inequality Having chosen $i$ independent vectors, the $(i+1)$-st must avoid their span, a subspace of exactly $p^{i}$ elements. So the number of independent $k$-tuples is $\prod_{i At the experimental scale — $p = 2$, ambient width $n = 192$, $k \le 8$ — the genericity loss is about $2^{-184}$. The exclusive dimensions are exclusive; the model isn't vacuous. But notice the *direction*. Reliability error shrinks like $p^{-k}$; genericity error **grows** like $p^{k-n}$. Combining them, the probability that the boundary token both occupies a genuinely $k$-dimensional subspace *and* escapes every obstruction is at least $$f(k) = 1 - \frac{m}{p^{k}} - \frac{p^{k}-1}{(p-1)p^{n}}.$$ Two opposed geometric forces, hence a smooth **interior** optimum near $k \approx n/2$ — and this is the deepest structural reason the reliability curve cannot be a cliff. A cliff is what a single monotone force produces. Here two forces act. {{visualization:1}} {{algorithm:3}}
The genericity certificate, in exact rational arithmetic {{algorithm:2}}

What is the **total failure mass** of the ramp, summed over all widths? $$\sum_{k \ge 0} p^{-k} = \frac{p}{p-1} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{p}\right)^{-1}.$$ That is the local [Euler factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_product) of the Riemann zeta function at $p$.
